mcqs.question: In Lomuto's partition scheme, what does index `i` track as `j` scans forward?
options: The position of the pivot before it's moved
The number of elements swapped so far
The midpoint of the current subarray
The right boundary of the region already confirmed to be less than the pivot
mcqs.explanation: `i` marks the last index known to hold an element less than the pivot; every time `j` finds another such element, `i` advances by one and the two are swapped, growing the confirmed "less than pivot" region by exactly one slot. It has nothing to do with the pivot's original position, a swap count, or the midpoint.

mcqs.question: Why does Hoare's partition scheme typically perform fewer swaps than Lomuto's?
options: It only swaps two elements when both are confirmed to be on the wrong side of the pivot, rather than swapping on every element found less than the pivot
It skips the partitioning step entirely for half of the array
It uses a hash table to avoid comparisons
It never swaps the pivot itself, only the elements around it
mcqs.explanation: Hoare's two pointers only swap when the left pointer has found something too large and the right pointer has found something too small — both elements are provably misplaced. Lomuto swaps every time it finds an element less than the pivot, even when that element might already sit close to correct, resulting in roughly 3x more swaps on average.

mcqs.question: Why does quicksort with a fixed last-element pivot hit O(n²) on an already-sorted array?
options: Because sorted arrays require more comparisons per element than random arrays
Because the partition step incorrectly reorders already-sorted elements
Because the pivot is always the current maximum, so every partition splits into sizes 1 and n-1, giving a recursion depth of n instead of log n
Because sorted input forces every comparison to be a tie
mcqs.explanation: On sorted input, the last element is always the largest in its range, so it partitions into a size-(n-1) side and an empty-ish side every single call — recursion depth n, each level doing O(n) work, for O(n²) total. Comparisons per element don't increase and there are no forced ties; the problem is purely the imbalance of the split.

mcqs.question: What does randomizing the pivot actually guarantee about quicksort's worst case?
options: It makes the O(n²) worst case mathematically impossible
It converts quicksort's worst case into an O(n) algorithm
It eliminates the need for recursion depth limits
It keeps the O(n²) worst case theoretically possible but makes its probability vanishingly small for any given input, and prevents an attacker from choosing an input that triggers it
mcqs.explanation: Randomization doesn't remove the worst case — an unlucky sequence of random choices could still hit it — but the probability shrinks exponentially with input size, and because the pivot depends on runtime randomness rather than input values, no attacker can construct a fixed array that reliably triggers it. It doesn't change the algorithm's asymptotic class or its recursion-depth behavior on its own.

mcqs.question: Why does naive Lomuto partitioning degrade to O(n²) on an array where every element is equal, while Hoare's scheme handles it well?
options: Lomuto's pivot never gets confirmed as "less than" by any element, so the partition puts almost everything on one side every time, while Hoare's opposite-end pointers still cross near the middle
Lomuto cannot handle duplicate values at all and throws an error
Hoare's scheme skips duplicate elements entirely
Lomuto requires the array to be pre-deduplicated before sorting
mcqs.explanation: With all-equal elements, Lomuto's `arr[j] < pivot` check is never true, so `i` never advances and the pivot ends up placed at one extreme end every call — a 1-vs-(n-1) split repeated all the way down, giving O(n²). Hoare's pointers, moving from opposite ends and stopping on `<` / `>` conditions relative to the pivot, still meet roughly in the middle on uniform data, giving a balanced split.

mcqs.question: You implement Hoare's partition but recurse with `quicksort(lo, p-1)` and `quicksort(p+1, hi)`, the bounds that go with Lomuto. What's the risk?
options: Nothing changes — the two schemes' returned indices mean the same thing
The sort becomes unstable

An element at index p can be excluded from both recursive calls, and in the case where the partition puts everything on one side, the same range can be passed to recursion unchanged, causing infinite recursion
The partition step runs twice as slowly
mcqs.explanation: Hoare's returned index is a partition boundary, not a guarantee that the pivot sits there — using Lomuto's `p-1`/`p+1` bounds can drop the element at `p` from ever being sorted, and in the degenerate case where `p` equals `hi`, the left call becomes `quicksort(lo, hi)` again, recursing forever. Hoare's correct bounds are `[lo, p]` and `[p+1, hi]`.
